**Walk: The whole piece** (working notes)

First read: the eye lands on "Landing stage rebuild" at the top left, then goes to the blue "Sign up" button on the right and to the flat blue-grey illustration. It reads as a ferry operator's news page with a box to sign up for timetable alerts. It feels calm, civic and plain. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash is refused in this session, so I could not crop or open entries with the script.

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? **yes**
- Do the main image and the headline make one idea together? **no**. The illustration (96–656, 220–420) is flat blocks: a grey slab, a dark bar and a blue rounded bar on pale water. It does not show the ramps, the covered waiting area, the benches or the kiosk that the headline and text describe.
- Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job? **yes**
- Do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era? **yes**
- Is the copy finished? **unsure**. The large copy is clean. The micro text (field labels, caption, form note, footer) is too small to read in this still, and I could not crop it.
- Within one screen, does each kind of element look the same everywhere? **yes**
- Do colors, shapes, and directions carry the mood? **yes**
- Does each heading name what its section holds? **yes**

Deep read: the entries script could not run. I judged the remaining lines by eye. "Visual and headline" is a line about an off-list source, so it counts as taste or common sense. "Copy finished" has no catalog entry, and a still image this size cannot settle it without zooming, so it stays unsure.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The main image and the headline do not make one idea together.** This is the illustration at x 96–656, y 220–420, under the intro paragraph. The headline and text promise wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water and a kiosk. The picture is a few flat rectangles: a pale grey block, a dark grey bar, and a blue rounded bar on blue water. None of the promised things is visible or labelled. The reader looks to the picture to see what changed and learns nothing, so it reads as a placeholder or a generic "pier" icon. Worse, the blue bar uses the same blue as the "Sign up" button. That sends a small false signal that it might be clickable, or that it is the boat. Why: common sense. The catalog entry ("Visual and headline work together") is off-list, so I treat this as taste backed by reasoning. Fix: replace it with a photo of the rebuilt stage, or redraw it to show the ramp meeting the deck and the covered area, labelled directly. If it stays abstract, take the CTA blue out of it. Taste, close to a defect. Weight: major, because it is the only image and it carries the "what changed" story of the article.

**What's working.**
- The two jobs are cleanly separated. The article sits left in a ~560 px reading column, and the alert sign-up sits in its own bordered card on the right. A first-time viewer can say "news about the rebuilt landing, plus a way to get timetable alerts" in one sentence.
- The headings say what they hold. "Landing stage rebuild" and "Get timetable changes" name their content plainly. The second one names the benefit, not the action, so the reader knows what the sign-up gives them before they reach the button.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the copy is finished. The field labels above both inputs (y ≈135 and ≈200), the caption under the figure (y ≈437), the note under the button (y ≈325) and the footer line (y ≈757) render at a few pixels and cannot be read here. Zoom in on them to check for placeholder text or typos. Their size is a matter for the Text critic.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea), 1 unsure (copy finished: micro text unreadable in the still)

Walk (working notes): first read: the eye lands on "Landing stage rebuild" at the top left (about 34 px bold). It then drops to the intro, the illustration and the blue "Sign up" button, and crosses to the card heading "Get timetable changes". The page reads as a ferry or harbour news item with an email signup beside it, and feels calm and plain. The job, assumed: tell passengers about the rebuilt landing stage and get sign-ups for timetable alerts.

- One element dominates: **yes**. The H1 is the largest and darkest type and sits top left. The card heading (about 22 px) is a clear step below it, and the illustration is pale, so it doesn't compete.
- Distinct text levels, no near-equal sizes: **yes**. I see title about 34, card heading about 22 bold, body about 18, button about 16 bold, and a micro level of about 4 px (field labels, figure caption, fine print, footer). Card heading and body are only about 4 px apart, but weight separates them. The micro level is a size and readability problem, which belongs to the Text section, not here.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes**. Both headings are bold against regular body text.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director (this section has no line for it; it belongs to the Text section): the field labels ("Your name", "Email address"), the figure caption at about (96, 437), the fine print under Sign up at about (789, 325) and the footer at about (96, 757) all look about 4 px tall. They're unreadable at normal viewing distance. The field labels matter most, because without them the two inputs at (789, 143) and (789, 207) have no name a user can read.

**What's working.**
- The title is clearly in charge. "Landing stage rebuild" is the biggest, darkest type and sits where reading starts, so the eye knows where to begin and the signup card comes second.
- The levels are separated by weight as well as size. Both headings are bold against regular body text, so the card heading reads as a heading even though it's only a few pixels bigger than the body.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**. The image is about 1280×800, about one screen. Bash is denied, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts and worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on the "Landing stage rebuild" H1, goes down to the paragraph and the illustration, then jumps right to the bordered "Get timetable changes" card and its blue button. This looks like an article page from a ferry operator with a sign-up sidebar. It feels calm and sparse, and everything sits in the top two-thirds.

1. One grid: **no**. The illustration (x 96–656) stops about 30 px short of the text column's right edge (about 686), so the picture doesn't take its width from the column. The left margin is 96 and the right margin is about 160.
2. Exact alignment, no near-misses: **no**. The card's top edge (y≈57) sits about 5 px above the H1's cap top (y≈62). It neither aligns nor clearly breaks.
3. Baselines across columns: yes. The card is a boxed aside.
4. Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes.
5. One group per box: yes.
6. Only related elements look alike: **no**. The blue rounded bar in the illustration (496–606, 340–364) has the same blue and the same corner radius as the "Sign up" button.
7. Nothing overlapping or touching: yes.
8. Margin from the edge: yes.
9. Empty space gathered: yes. It is one large area at the bottom right.
10. Balance: **no**. All the weight is above y≈510 and to the left. The right column is empty below y≈357, and the content block sits about 32 px left of the page's centre.
11. Centring by habit: yes. Nothing is centred.
12. One proportion for the main divisions: yes. The columns are roughly 3:2.
13. Eye path: yes.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?** The blue rounded bar in the illustration (about x 496–606, y 340–364) uses the same saturated blue and corner radius as the "Sign up" button (789–888, 263–307). Those two are the only saturated blue on the page, so they pair up. The bar reads as an unlabelled second button sitting in the article column, which looks broken, and it pulls attention away from the real action. (Gestalt similarity: Arnheim; Refactoring UI. I couldn't open the entry to confirm.) Fix: change the boat's colour or shape so it can't be mistaken for a control. A muted or different hue works, or a hull silhouette instead of a pill, so that the action blue belongs only to the action. Defect. Weight: minor.
2. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** The illustration's right edge (x≈656) doesn't match the main column. The body text runs out to about 686 above and below it, so the picture looks almost full-width but not quite. The page margins are also uneven: 96 px on the left and about 160 px on the right. Fix: set the picture to the full text-column width, or clearly narrower. Then either use the same outer margin on both sides or make the left alignment obviously intentional. Convention (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*). Weight: minor.
3. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** The card's top border (y≈57) is about 5 px above the H1's cap height (y≈62). The two column tops look almost aligned, which reads as a slip. Fix: align the card's top edge to the H1's cap height, or drop the card clearly lower, for example to the first paragraph. Convention. Weight: minor.
4. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All content ends at y≈510 in the left column and y≈357 in the right. The lower third is empty apart from a tiny footer line at y≈757, and the right column below the card is bare. The page feels top-left heavy, and the footer looks stranded. This is partly normal for a short article on a tall viewport, so I'm treating it as taste. Fix: either let the article and the card fill more of the frame, or bring the footer up to sit a set distance below the content. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The space inside each group is clearly smaller than the space between groups. The caption sits tight under the illustration, the paragraphs sit near their neighbours, and inside the card each label sits close to its field with more space before the next one, so the groups read at a glance. The two-column split, at roughly 3:2 with a clear gutter of about 70 px, separates the article from the sign-up aside without any rule lines.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the card stays in view on scroll and how the two columns stack on narrow widths. Both matter here because the sign-up is the page's only action.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (one grid; exact alignment or clearly off; only related elements look alike; balance), 0 unsure. The entries script couldn't be run because Bash was denied, so these findings rest on the checklist and the canon rather than on the opened entries.

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are captions, labels, and legal text large enough to read?** No. Five pieces of small text are about 3–4 px tall, and none of them can be read at this size:
   - the "Your name" label above the first field (about x789, y135);
   - the label above the second field (about x789, y200);
   - the helper line under Sign up (x789–915, y325), which looks like it says how often you'll be emailed and how to stop;
   - the figure caption under the picture (x96–186, y437);
   - the footer note (x96–215, y758).

   **What the viewer meets:** two empty boxes with no readable label, so they have to guess what goes in each one. One field is probably the name, but the other could be an email address or a choice of route. The sign-up promise is unreadable at exactly the moment they're asked to commit. They can't tell what the picture shows, and the footer disclaimer may as well not be there.

   **Why:** Apple's Human Interface Guidelines set 11 pt as the smallest text on iOS. This text is roughly a third of that.

   **Fix:** bring all of it up to the page's small size. The label and helper text should be about 14 px, or close to body size. Keep the labels in the darker text colour. Once they're readable, check that the grey helper, caption and footer text reaches 4.5:1 contrast (WCAG 1.4.3), because at this size the anti-aliasing makes them look paler than their actual colour.

   Defect. Weight: major. The form can't be filled in with confidence, and its commitment line can't be read.

**What's working.**
- The body paragraph is a good reading size: it looks about 18 px with comfortable leading, and lines run about 70 characters (x96–683). That's within Bringhurst's 45–75, so it reads easily.
- There is one sans-serif family throughout, and the scale steps are clear: the headline, the card heading, body, and the bold button. Nothing collides, and keeping those steps distinct is what makes the fix above easy. Use one more step for the small text rather than inventing a new size.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (captions and labels large enough to read). The weight and contrast lines are counted as yes because the faintness comes from the tiny size and is filed under the captions line.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(A note for the director, not a colour-line failure: the boat in the illustration (about x 496–606, y 340–364) uses the same saturated blue as the "Sign up" button (x 789–888, y 263–307), and it is also a rounded rectangle. At first glance it reads like a second button. The checklist's status-colour line only covers misused red, green, amber and blue status meanings, so I answered it yes. If this belongs anywhere, it belongs under "pictures" or "interface", as a figure that looks clickable. The fix would be to give the boat a different colour or shape, so the saturated blue appears only on the one action.)

**What's working.**
- The palette is tight: one blue-gray neutral range and a single saturated blue. That blue covers well under 5% of the page, which keeps the page calm and makes "Sign up" the only strong colour in the side panel (Refactoring UI; Albers on restraint).
- The value structure holds up in grayscale. The near-black text and headline, the mid-gray deck, and the pale sky and water stay distinct, so the illustration and the page structure still read without hue.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

I checked the one illustration on the page against the Pictures checklist. It fails two of the 12 lines and passes the rest.

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one illustration, at about x 96–656, y 220–420, with a caption under it.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. The illustration is four flat shapes: a pale sky band, a pale grey block, a dark grey slab, a blue rounded bar and a blue water band. It reads as a wireframe placeholder, not a finished picture. The text just above it promises wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water and a kiosk. The text below it is about ramps meeting the deck at every tide. None of that is drawn. The reader has to guess that the slab is the landing stage, the grey block is the shelter and the blue bar is the boat. It adds no information the text doesn't already give, and makes the page look unfinished. The catalog has no entry for this line, so this is common sense. Direction of fix: show what the rebuild changed, at least the ramp meeting the boat deck and the covered waiting area, in a recognisable form. A real photo of the new stage would do this best. If it really is a placeholder, replace it before publishing. Defect. **Weight: major.** This is the article's only picture, and it fails to show the rebuild the article is about.
2. **Does the subject of each picture stand clearly apart from its background?** No. The pale grey block at about x 176–296, y 280–330 (presumably the covered waiting area) is very close in value to the pale blue-grey sky behind it, so it almost disappears. The blue boat at about x 496–606, y 340–364 is also only a step darker than the water it sits across. The only shape with a clear edge is the dark slab. The eye therefore takes in "a grey bar on water" and misses the shelter, which is one of the two features the text names. The catalog's source for this entry is not on the approved list, so this is argued as common sense. Direction of fix: give each part of the subject a clear step in value from what is behind it. For example, darken or outline the shelter against the sky and separate the boat from the water. Defect. **Weight: minor** on its own, but it adds to finding 1.

**What's working.**
- The picture is sharp, flat and undistorted, at a clean width that lines up with the text column (left edge x 96, about 560 px wide). It sits on the page's grid instead of fighting it.
- Its one rendering style and one level of detail have no fake depth or texture, so it doesn't compete with the headline.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 10 yes, 2 no (every image shows its content; subject stands apart from its background), 0 unsure

**Findings**

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a signup form with two text fields and a "Sign up" button in the right-hand card (x 760–1120, y 56–356).

**Findings**
1. **Does every field have its own visible label, closer to it than to any other field, not a placeholder alone?** (also answers no to **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen?**) Each field has a label above it, at about x 789, y 135 and y 200. Both labels are only about 4 px tall, which is unreadable at normal viewing distance. Even a full-resolution crop shows only a smudge that might say "Your name" and "Home landing". A visitor sees two empty boxes and a button, and has to guess what goes in each one. Neither box seems to ask for an email address or a phone number, so it's also unclear how the "timetable changes" would reach them. The label is there in principle, but it does nothing, so the field is as good as unlabelled (NN/g, Sherwin, "Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful"; WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions). Fix: set the labels at least at body size (about 14–16 px), in the dark text colour, directly above each field. Check that the fields ask for what a notification needs, which is a contact address plus the landing. Defect, **major**: this form is the only action on the page and can't be filled in with confidence.
2. **Are required or optional fields marked?** Neither field shows an asterisk or the word "optional", so the visitor can't tell whether both must be filled in. With only two fields the cost is small. Fix: mark the optional field "(optional)", or put asterisks on the required ones and explain the asterisk once (Budiu, NN/g, "Marking Required Fields in Forms"). Convention, **minor**.
3. **Do the inputs allow only valid values, by pickers, input types, or disabled options?** The second field (y 207–247) looks like it is labelled "Home landing", but it's a plain text box. The visitor has to type a landing name and can misspell it or use a name the system doesn't know. A select or set of options listing the landings would rule that out (Nielsen, heuristic 5, error prevention). If the label actually asks for something open-ended, this is fine. Defect, **minor**.

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one action, the solid blue "Sign up" button (about 99×44 px, x 789–888, y 263–307). It's clearly the primary action, large enough to hit, and nothing competes with it.
- The fields have dark, full borders and generous height, so they read as places to type at a glance. The form is a single column in its own card, separate from the article, so it's obvious this is a self-contained task.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether a focused field or the button shows a visible focus indicator at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast. This matters because keyboard users have to move between the two fields and the button.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 4 no (one primary... n/a; field labels visible; everything needed visible; required fields marked; inputs allow only valid values), 1 unsure (focus indicator)

Corrected tally: `Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 4 no (inputs allow only valid values; everything needed visible on this screen; every field has its own visible label; required or optional fields marked), 1 unsure (focused control shows an indicator)`
